doc.title: Clyde Kerr Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 22, 2006

title: Explaining the second line and the music at a jazz funeral
summary: Dirges on the way to the grave, lively tunes after, the family as first line and onlookers as second line; religion makes no difference outside the church.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Jazz funerals: dirges, hot return, second line

blocks.x: Someone who’s not at all familiar with the term “second line” or “second liners,” can you describe how that happens and what it’s like?

Yeah. When a person passes, when they die, the tradition is the jazz funeral in which the family — we have a procession that goes to the gravesite and there’s a brass band that’s playing, what we call dirges, which is a slow, very slow song, it’s moving, very slow and very solemn-like. It’s not the time to play any happy type music because it’s a sad occasion. So there’s a group of the family members walking in the street behind the hearse or the casket, and there are onlookers who are marching behind them. So after the person is entombed and the family moves on and goes back home then the brass band strikes up a lively type of tune and everybody starts dancing, and it’s the people. There’s the first line with the family, the second line is the onlookers, so they start dancing and having a good time. Because actually they say you’re supposed to rejoice when a person dies, and really cry when a person is born because they have to go through the pain of life you know. So death is like a blessing in some ways, and it makes sense. It makes sense because the person who moved on, they don’t have to suffer the things they have to suffer in this particular life you know. They’re going on to their reward. So the band strikes up this lively tune and everybody with umbrellas and handkerchiefs are having a good time and they’re rejoicing. So that is the second line.
How does the person’s particular religion kind of jive with this? Does it make a difference if a person is Episcopalian or if he’s Baptist?

No I don’t think so. I don’t think so. Basically the jazz funerals were sort of designated from musicians so it didn’t make any sense. Because you have a service going on in the church and then outside there’s another thing going on. So whatever goes on in the church, that’s that service or whatever. Outside it has no denomination whatsoever. And so usually outside there are people talking and the brass band around waiting, and you know just waiting for the service inside the church to come out. So sometimes I used to stay in the church if I really was close to the person, I want to be there for the services, whatever, if I knew the person well but not necessarily that I needed to be inside that church. To be outside is another thing to be a part of that because of the conversations that’s going on outside with other musicians and people. And I mean actually I would like to be both places. So sometimes you have to make a choice of being in the church or being outside because things are happening both places. So I’ve been both places. And man it’s something that happens that doesn’t happen anywhere in the world but New Orleans the way it does. I have experience, like when I evacuated New Orleans I went outside of Atlanta, Georgia, a place called Acworth, Georgia by one of my daughters.
